extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents/applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing patent-eligibility analyses under MPEP §2106.04, focusing on laws of nature, natural phenomena, products of nature, and the markedly different characteristics analysis used to determine whether claimed nature-based products are judicial exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract ideas / mathematical formulas as judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical formula (e.g., the Arrhenius equation) is an exception like a scientific principle or natural phenomenon and is non-statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims directed to mathematical formulas, algorithms, or similar abstract concepts are treated as judicial exceptions and are not patent eligible per se. See Diehr, Benson, Flook, Mackay, Bilski, and related case law. If a claim recites such an exception, it is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further analysis in Step 2B to determine whether the claim recites a patent-eligible application of the exception. Examples include algorithms for converting binary coded decimal to pure binary (Benson), formulas for computing alarm limits (Flook), and mathematical formulas for hedging (Bilski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts involving performing mathematical calculations can be abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that involve generating values, calculating policy or investment values, manipulating numerical results, or organizing information through mathematical correlations may be directed to abstract ideas of performing mathematical computations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found claims abstract where they describe mere mathematical computation or manipulation of data (e.g., Bancorp, Digitech). Examiners should look to the specification to determine whether claimed determinations are 'mere mathematical computation' and consider these as abstract ideas under Step 2A (requiring Step 2B if the claim is otherwise directed to a judicial exception). Examples include calculating surrender value credits (Bancorp) and organizing existing information into a new form via mathematical formulas (Digitech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena are judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or that do not have markedly different characteristics compared to what occurs in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The courts treat basic tools of scientific and technological work (laws of nature, natural phenomena) as part of the storehouse of knowledge and not patentable. Examples include isolated DNA (Myriad), cloned animals (Roslin), correlations between biomarkers and disease (Mayo, Cleveland Clinic), electromagnetism (O’Reilly v. Morse), and cell-free fetal DNA (Ariosa). Not every claim describing a natural ability or quality is necessarily 'directed to' a law of nature (e.g., treatment methods may be eligible). A claim reciting a law of nature or natural phenomenon is considered directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires Step 2B analysis for an eligible application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of nature exception for nature-based products
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law of nature or natural phenomenon is claimed as a physical product, it is often treated as a 'product of nature' exception and can be ineligible unless it possesses markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Products of nature include both naturally occurring products and non-naturally occurring products that are structurally identical to natural counterparts. Synthetic replication does not automatically confer eligibility (Ambry Genetics; Myriad). The key is whether the claimed nature-based product possesses markedly different characteristics from any naturally occurring counterpart. If a claim recites a nature-based product limitation, examiners should use the markedly different characteristics analysis (MPEP §2106.04(c)) to evaluate whether the limitation is a product of nature exception. Examples: isolated genes, primers, cloned animals, genetically modified bacteria (Chakrabarty, Roslin, Myriad, Ambry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (part of Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis compares the nature-based product limitation to its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state to determine whether the product is a 'product of nature' exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Markedly different characteristics can be expressed as the product’s structure, function, and/or other properties and are evaluated on a claim-by-claim basis. If the nature-based product limitation has markedly different characteristics, the claim does not recite a product of nature exception (Step 2A: NO) at Pathway B unless another exception is present; if it does not, the limitation is a product of nature exception (Step 2A: YES) and the claim requires Step 2B analysis to determine whether additional elements add significantly more. For claims that are only a single nature-based product, showing a markedly different characteristic obviates further analysis (no Step 2B needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to apply the markedly different characteristics analysis — product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims to a nature-based product by itself (e.g., 'a Lactobacillus bacterium'), apply the markedly different characteristics analysis to the entire product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the claim is to a nature-based product as a whole, compare that entire claimed product to the closest naturally occurring counterpart (e.g., Chakrabarty's bacterium). For combinations of components producing a resultant nature-based combination (e.g., a probiotic composition comprising Lactobacillus and milk), analyze the resultant combination rather than each component separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to apply the markedly different characteristics analysis — product-in-combination and product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claim recites a nature-based product in combination with non-nature-based elements, or is a product-by-process claim, the analysis focuses on the nature-based product limitation's characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a nature-based product in combination with non-nature elements (e.g., a yogurt starter kit comprising Lactobacillus plus container/instructions), analyze only the nature-based product limitation for markedly different characteristics; other elements are considered in Step 2B if the nature-based product is a product of nature. For product-by-process claims, the question is whether the nature-based product in the claim has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart (see MPEP §2113).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to apply the markedly different characteristics analysis — process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, process claims are not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis because the focus should be on active steps of the process rather than products used in those steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate process claims based on the process steps (e.g., cryopreserving hepatocytes was eligible because it was a process of creating a preparation, Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect). However, if a process claim is drafted so that there is no substantive difference from a product claim (i.e., it effectively claims the product), then the claim is subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis (example: 'a method of providing an apple' focuses on the apple product and should be treated accordingly). Claims to mere detection of naturally occurring entities (e.g., detecting cffDNA) can be directed to the natural phenomenon itself and thus fall under product-of-nature analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step in the markedly different characteristics analysis is selecting the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart(s) to the nature-based product limitation for comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature-based product is derived from a naturally occurring thing, use that naturally occurring thing as the counterpart (e.g., deoxyacid A derived from acid A). The counterpart should be in its natural state and not conflated with adjacent natural material (e.g., compare an isolated gene to the gene, not the entire chromosome). When multiple potential counterparts exist, compare to the closest naturally occurring counterpart (using examiner expertise). For claimed combinations with no natural counterpart, the closest counterparts may be the individual components (e.g., bacterial mixtures compared to individual species). If the claim is rejected as ineligible, it is best practice for the examiner to identify the selected counterpart in the Office action if not already clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying and evaluating characteristics for 'markedly different'
rubrics_metrics.description: Markedly different characteristics may be expressed as differences in structure, function, and/or other properties, and must be evaluated based on what is recited in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claimed nature-based product limitation to the selected naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state on the basis of structure, function, and other properties recited in the claim. If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, no markedly different characteristics analysis is needed because it is by definition a naturally occurring product. If the limitation is not naturally occurring (e.g., modified by human intervention), perform the analysis to determine whether it possesses markedly different characteristics sufficient to avoid the product-of-nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) considerations and claim narrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Under BRI, a nature-based product limitation may encompass both eligible and ineligible products; examiners should consider BRI and recommend narrowing amendments where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the BRI of a claim may cover embodiments that lack markedly different characteristics, a claim may be directed to a product of nature under Step 2A. If a claim is directed to products both with and without markedly different characteristics, examiners should point out the BRI and, where possible, recommend an amendment to narrow the claim to embodiments that are not directed to products of nature or that are otherwise eligible. Example: a claim to 'a cloned giraffe' may have a BRI encompassing cloned giraffes with and without markedly different characteristics; examiners should identify this and suggest narrowing amendments in Office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined eligibility analysis when claims do not seek to tie up exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim that recites a nature-based product limitation clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception, consider whether the streamlined eligibility analysis in MPEP §2106.06 is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims that recite nature-based products but are clearly directed to inventions that do not attempt to preempt the use of the judicial exception, examiners may apply a streamlined eligibility analysis and may not need to perform the full markedly different characteristics analysis. Examiners should consider this approach where appropriate to avoid unnecessary analysis.
